API returns category: "podcast" but CLI enum does not include it

Readwise API can return documents with category: "podcast". The CLI's DocumentInfo Pydantic model only allows: article, email, rss, highlight, note, pdf, epub, tweet, video. Any list that includes a podcast document fails with a validation error before results are shown. Workaround: use --category article (or another single category) so the API only returns that category—but then see layout bug below.

Layout code assumes document["category"]; KeyError when printing

When list fetches documents and passes them to table_layout() or list_layout(), the code does document["category"] == "highlight" or document["category"] == "note" but the dict passed in does not always have a "category" key. Result: KeyError: 'category' and the command exits even when the API returned data. Observed with both --layout table and --layout list. So even with --category article (which avoids the podcast enum error), the CLI can still crash at the print step.

SAE J3016 Levels of Driving Automation

The standard that sorts self-driving cars into six levels, from 0 (no automation) to 5 (drives anywhere with no human). Regulators, carmakers and the press use these levels to describe what a car can do on its own.
SAE J3016 Levels of Driving Automation
SAE J3016 Levels of Driving Automation
The levels describe the driving automation system, not the car. One car can run at Level 2 on city streets and Level 3 in a highway traffic jam.
SAE J3016 Levels of Driving Automation
The key line falls between Level 2 and Level 3. Through Level 2 the human is driving and must watch the road at all times. From Level 3 up the system is driving while it is engaged.

Level 0 of SAE/J3016. The system can warn or briefly intervene, as with automatic emergency braking or blind-spot warnings. The human drives.
Level 1 of SAE/J3016. The system steers or controls speed, as with adaptive cruise control or lane centering alone. The human drives.
Level 2 of SAE/J3016. The system steers and controls speed together. The human must supervise constantly and take over at once.
GM Super Cruise and Ford BlueCruise, which allow hands-off driving on mapped highways while a camera checks that the driver watches the road
Level 3 of SAE/J3016. The system drives within a limited domain, such as a highway below a set speed. The human may look away but must take over when the system asks.
Mercedes-Benz Drive Pilot, the first Level 3 system certified in Germany and in the US states of California and Nevada
BMW Personal Pilot L3 on the 7 Series in Germany
Level 4 of SAE/J3016. The system drives with no human in a limited area or set of conditions, such as a mapped city. If something goes wrong it pulls over on its own. Most robotaxis sit here.
Waymo, from Alphabet, runs driverless rides in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin and other cities
Zoox, from Amazon, runs a purpose-built robotaxi with no steering wheel in Las Vegas, with a smaller public service in San Francisco
Baidu Apollo Go, Pony.ai and WeRide run driverless robotaxis in China
Cruise, from GM, ran driverless rides in San Francisco until GM shut the robotaxi business down in December 2024
Level 5 of SAE/J3016. The system drives anywhere a human could, in all conditions. No production system has reached Level 5.

Satisfice means to accept the first option that meets a minimum standard instead of searching for the best one. It is a portmanteau of satisfy and suffice, coined by Person/Herbert A. Simon in 1956.
Source words: satisfy, for meeting a need, and suffice, for being enough.
"Satisfice" was already in use in the 1500s as a northern variant of satisfy, with the earliest documented use in 1561. Simon gave the old spelling a new meaning.
Simon's book Administrative Behavior (1947) was his first major book, on administrative decision making.

In "A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice" (1955) he described choosing among alternatives by a two-valued payoff, satisfactory or unsatisfactory, with the boundary at an "aspiration level." His example was a house seller who regards $15,000 as acceptable, anything over it as satisfactory and anything under it as unsatisfactory.
"Rational Choice and the Structure of the Environment" appeared in Psychological Review 63(2) in March 1956.
Simon argued that "organisms adapt well enough to 'satisfice'; they do not, in general, 'optimize.'"
He described a choice mechanism that pursues "a 'satisficing' path, a path that will permit satisfaction at some specified level of all of its needs."
He thanked Person/Allen Newell for "numerous enlightening conversations on the subject of this paper."

Satisficing became the standard example of bounded rationality: decision makers have limited information and limited capacity to compute, so a rule that stops at "good enough" is a rational response, not a failure.
Simon's 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded "for his pioneering research into the decision-making process within economic organizations."

Simon came to believe that a theory of decision making needed a theory of human problem solving, studied through computer programs. In 1955 he, Person/Allen Newell and J. Clifford Shaw created Logic Theorist, which used heuristic rules to prove theorems, and Simon and Newell shared the 1975 Turing Award.
In 2002 Person/Barry Schwartz and co-authors published "Maximizing versus satisficing: happiness is a matter of choice" in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

The paper reported a Maximization Scale that measures the desire to maximize. Maximizing correlated negatively with happiness, optimism, self-esteem and life satisfaction, and positively with depression, perfectionism and regret.
Schwartz carried the distinction into The Paradox of Choice: Why More Is Less (2004), where too many options make choosing harder and outcomes feel worse.

Person/Gerd Gigerenzer, Peter M. Todd and the ABC Research Group presented simple decision rules as a psychologically realistic account of bounded rationality in Simple Heuristics That Make Us Smart (1999).
